column1: 00:15|Good afternoon, dear friends. Please welcome editor-in-chief Dmitry Mikhailovich Borisenko.
00:20|Greetings.
00:21|Hello, Pavel, and greetings to your viewers and my subscribers.
00:29|I'm glad that Pavel Ivanov, a designated foreign agent, and I can finally continue our regular conversations.
00:37|Dmitry Mikhailovich, let's get straight to it. During our previous conversation, we raised the issue of mobilization.
00:46|We agreed that there appeared to be no specific confirmed information. I'm quoting Sobchak's outlet, Ostorozhno Moskva:
00:59|In Moscow, a man walking his dog was taken to a military enlistment office and is being prepared for military service.
01:05|His lawyer says the conscription process has involved violations and the man hasn't even had a medical examination.
01:12|According to Dmitry's family, a local police officer stopped him while he was walking his dog on the morning of November 5.
01:20|He was allowed to take the dog home, then taken to a military enlistment office and afterwards to a police department.
01:25|According to the lawyer, officers initially cited Article 19.3 of the administrative code, concerning disobedience of a police officer's lawful order,
01:32|but administrative proceedings were not initiated. It's a long and very strange story.
01:42|We've heard of people caught, for example, placing illegal drug packages, and instead of being sent to prison, they are sent elsewhere.
01:55|But what does this have to do with mobilization, or is it the police? What is the connection? Police don't work for military enlistment offices.
02:06|But something else is more interesting. Sobchak has a larger outlet, Ostorozhno Novosti, with 1.5 million subscribers, and a personal channel.
02:16|The story wasn't discussed there. But other outlets reported that Sobchak has legal and tax problems
02:24|and faces a two-year ban on registering new companies. I wonder: did she touch on a dangerous subject and receive a hint to keep quiet?
02:43|I wouldn't be surprised, Pavel. Another blogger, Romanov, a so-called war correspondent, recently covered the situation in Oleshky.
03:02|After that he stopped communicating. Some say he may have been detained and could face charges, from spreading alleged false information about the army to treason.
03:14|Opinions differ. As we've often discussed, nobody in our country can now be completely protected by powerful connections.
03:30|Someone might claim protection in the FSO, FSB, Interior Ministry or Investigative Committee. But that hasn't worked for a long time.
03:44|What's more, announcing it publicly could prompt an even quicker detention. Competition among the security services is growing.
04:04|I believe their leaders aren't working toward a common goal but for their own survival. They regard one another with suspicion. The situation is tense.
04:22|So even Sobchak's close connections, including her relationship with General Zolotov and personal contacts with the president, may not protect her.
04:54|That is, if action is sanctioned from the top, or initiated by a security agency that decides she should be silenced.
05:14|Why should they look back at Zolotov, Bortnikov or anyone else? They no longer defer to names as they once did.
05:27|Who are these forces? People keep asking me whether I'm really a foreign agent and whether I've left the country.
05:37|Today someone offered me a theory: I was supposedly asked to inform on or set up a dangerous woman, refused, and was designated a foreign agent as a result.
05:54|That's the first I've heard of it, yet people say a serious person told them. Who are these people? Is it everyone against everyone?
06:15|Everyone against everyone, exactly. We don't know who is behind the action concerning Sobchak.
06:34|Apparently they decided they needn't defer to the heads of other security agencies, believing they are acting within their authority and the law.
06:52|So many laws have been passed that anyone can now be pursued under one law or another. That is enough for them.
07:02|As for the explanation of your foreign-agent designation and departure: I've heard two theories. Yours is the third. Cherchez la femme — look for the woman.
07:27|Perhaps you should start collecting these stories about yourself. — I try to keep track.
07:35|— What are your two theories? — The first, perhaps from someone around you, was that Putin was told Pavel Ivanov had said the emperor has no clothes.
07:53|The second was that your criticism crossed Umar Kremlev, an influential person, who allegedly took administrative steps leading to your designation.
08:12|Now a woman has appeared in the third version. There are probably another three or four on the way.
08:24|— There are even more. Some said Borisenko, a friend of Karaulov, says dangerous things; Karaulov was designated, so Borisenko would be next.
08:40|Thank God that hasn't happened to you yet. But Sobchak was a presidential candidate, knows Putin and his family personally and has connections.
09:03|— These are troubled times. Everything is in confusion. It's sad that we're forced to discuss rumors
09:32|that have nothing to do with improving people's welfare or democratic reforms. We're discussing something absurd.
09:47|Five minutes before our conversation, I heard a quote from Dugin. At first I was convinced the video was AI-generated.
09:59|— I'll insert the Dugin quote here.
10:03|— We have all lost a great deal in this war. I want to address everyone who is still on the other side.
10:11|We love and respect you. Even if we are forced to kill you, shooting our own brothers and sisters in the heart, face or head,
10:25|we do it for a very important purpose. We cannot even fully comprehend that purpose; it exceeds all our declared objectives.
10:40|We do it in the name of salvation and transformation. We are one with you.
10:53|— I was shocked, because Dugin is still in demand among people at the top.
